This single fascicle of scripture is like the *Analects* of the Confucian tradition: while its words are finite, its principles are inexhaustible.

Since the Buddha-dharma came from the West, although this text has been recorded within the five hundred and seventy-seventh fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, its literary meaning has [passed through] six...
The Dharma Master of the Tang dynasty translated what is currently in circulation; however, this is actually the version by Kumārajīva of the Qin.
The commentaries and discussions preceding and following it are not uniform; only Chan Master Zongmi of Caotang attained the most [insight]. Observing his preface, it says:
"Dwelling in seventeen places, he secretly revealed the gradations; severing twenty-seven doubts, he subtly connected the vital veins, reaching even unto wisdom."

The teaching that "penetrating the three emptinesses encompasses the myriad practices" is not easily reached unless one is profound in Prajñā; it would be difficult to attain such an understanding otherwise.
The assembly leader Zhengjiang Liu and the patron for the fundraising, Master Fan Rong, recently obtained this text and had it carved onto woodblocks at Qiao-an, requesting me to compose a preface.
Now, the World-Honored One expounded the Prajñā in four locations and sixteen assemblies; this [text] is from the Jetavana Grove...

Answer: This is the ninth assembly of Subhūti. It has been carved for the sake of all virtuous people; one must forget the trap to catch the rabbit, yet even the Master of the River (Laozi) could not avoid adding feet to a painted snake.
Written on the day of the commencement of the retreat in the Jihai year of the Chunxi era by West-Obscured (Xiyin) Wujie (Huizang), "The Inexhaustible One."
In the Invocation of the Vajracchedikā Sūtra:
If there be anyone who receives and upholds the Vajracchedikā Sūtra, they must first with sincere resolve recite the Mantra for Purifying Oral Karma;
thereafter, they shall invoke the names of the Eight Vajras and Four Bodhisattvas, so that these deities may constantly provide protection wherever [the practitioner] dwells.
The Mantra for Purifying Oral Karma:
*Sūri sūri mahāsūri sū sūri svāhā*.
The Verse for Opening the Sutra:

The unsurpassed, most profound, and subtle Dharma, Difficult to encounter in hundreds of thousands of millions of kalpas— I have now seen, heard, received, and upheld it; May I understand the true meaning of the Tathāgata.
*Commentary on the Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Volume One.
Regarding the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, Master Chuanshu said:
"Dharmas do not arise in isolation; who is it that bestows names upon them? The verse says:
The Great Dharma King, Neither short nor long, Primordially without black or white.
Appearing everywhere as blue and yellow, Flowers bloom to behold the morning’s splendor; Forests wither following the evening frost.
How too urgent is the swift thunder? Even the rapid lightning is no light. The nine sages still find it difficult to fathom;
How could dragons and devas measure it? People of past and present do not recognize it; Provisionally established, it is named Vajra.
(The original commentary is that which was set forth by the Sixth Patriarch; the verses and the glosses are those set forth by Master Chuandao).

New Commentary: This sutra uses a dual metaphor for its name, takes the true mark (*dharmatā*) as its essence, takes non-attachment as its thesis, takes the severing of doubt as its function, and takes the Mahāyāna as its doctrinal characteristic.
First, regarding the explanation of the name through the metaphor of the *vajra*: it is the metaphor of the diamond.
The Prajñā is the essence within gold—extremely firm and extremely sharp, capable of shattering all things.

Because this sutra can sever the doubts and attachments of sentient beings, it is taken as a metaphor. Thus, among the sixteen divisions of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*, this sutra is named the "Section on Severance" (*Cchedaka-vibhāga*).
*Pāramitā* is a Sanskrit term; its Chinese translation is "reaching the other shore" (*to-ban-di*). Sentient beings [cross over by means of it].
Within the ocean of birth and death, there is no end; by cultivating this *prajñā*, one reaches the other shore of *nirvāṇa*.
For a Mahāyāna Bodhisattva who realizes that birth and death are themselves *nirvāṇa*, there is neither crossing nor reaching—yet they cross and reach nonetheless.

Regarding the term "Sūtra": it is defined as "Dharma" and "Constant. In the Sanskrit language, it is called *sūtra*; this is translated here as "Scripture of Accordance" (*qijing*), meaning it accords with [the truth].

This is because the principle accords with the capacity [of the audience]. Second, regarding the discernment of the essence of the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), this refers to the single principle of the true mark.
As the Sūtra says: "If a person hears this sūtra, they will immediately give rise to the true mark. Third, regarding the clarification that non-abiding is the central tenet (*siddhānta*):
"tenet" means the essential point. As the Sūtra says: "One should abide nowhere. This is because throughout the sūtra, non-abiding is frequently used to refute attachment.
It takes non-abiding as its fundamental principle (*mūla*). Fourth, it takes the severing of doubt as its function (*prayojana*);

because the power and function of the sutra can sever deluded attachments, it takes the severing of doubt as its function. Fifth, it takes the Mahāyāna as its doctrinal characteristic (*śāsana-lakṣaṇa*);
because the sutra says, "It is taught for those of the Supreme Vehicle," it takes the Mahāyāna as its doctrinal characteristic. This sutra is...
The division into thirty-two sections, translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty, is traditionally said to have been established by Prince Zhaoming of the Liang dynasty;
however, this was not present in the original translation. Furthermore, its topical divisions differ from those of the root treatise (*mūla-śāstra*) and fragment the meaning of the sūtra;
therefore, it is not adopted here. The commentary now provided is based on one version of the verses by Maitreya and Vasubandhu.
This treatise extracts the essential meaning without employing the full wording, because those expressions are profound and difficult for beginners to grasp immediately.
Translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Kumārajīva of the Yao Qin dynasty under imperial decree.
Section One: The Origin of the Dharma Assembly. The Minister and Layman Zhang Wujin said:
"Without the Dharma, there is no means to discuss emptiness; without an assembly, there is no means to expound the Dharma.

The myriad phenomena stand in dense array—this is called the 'cause. That the single mind responds and gives rise to them is called the 'origin. Therefore, the discourse begins first with the Dharma."
The Section on the Causes of the Assembly.
Thus have I heard. "Thus" (evam) indicates the meaning; "I have heard" (śrutam) is a term of certainty. Ānanda refers to himself, saying: "In this manner, I [have heard] this Dharma from the Buddha."
Since the enlightened one does not speak for himself, it is said, "Thus have I heard. Furthermore, "I" refers to the nature (*xing*); nature is itself the self.
All internal and external activities arise from this nature, and because everything is heard through it, it is called "heard by me."
At one time the Buddha was staying in the Kingdom of Śrāvastī at the Jeta Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park.
“At one time” refers to the occasion when the teacher and his disciples met and assembled together. “The Buddha” refers to the master who preaches the Dharma.
“Was staying” (in) indicates the location. “The Kingdom of Śrāvastī” is the kingdom where King Prasenajit resided.
"Jeta" is the name of the prince; because this tree was bestowed by Prince Jeta, it is called "Jeta’s Tree.
"Givaka" (Sudatta) is an alternative name for the elder Anāthapiṇḍada; because the park originally belonged to Sudatta, it is called the "Givaka’s Garden" (Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park).
"Buddha" is a Sanskrit term; in the language of Tang (Chinese), it means "Awakened. There are two meanings of "awakening": first, the external...
To awaken to the emptiness of all dharmas in two ways: internally, one awakens to the mind as empty and quiescent, not being deeply affected by the six sense-objects;
externally, one does not see the faults or evils of others, nor is one internally deluded by perversions. Therefore, this is called "awakening," and awakening is itself the Buddha.
He was together with a great assembly of one thousand two hundred and fifty bhikṣus.

As for the word "together with" (yǔ): it is said that the Buddha was "together with" the bhikṣus because they resided together in the Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā, the Dharma-assembly of formlessness.
Regarding "great bhikṣu" (dà bǐqiū): these are the great arhats. Regarding "bhikṣu": this is a Sanskrit term; in the language of Tang (Chinese), it means...
One who is able to destroy the six thieves is called a bhikṣu; "many" refers to their great number. The figure of one thousand two hundred and fifty is the specific count.
"Together" means they are in the same place, at a dharma assembly of equality.
As the ancients said: "To call it 'suchness' (tathatā) is already to have altered it. Now tell me, where does this alteration go?
*Du!* Do not wander aimlessly. Ultimately, how would you say it? Fire has never burned the mouth. The verse says:
Like the solitary moon in the vast sky on a tranquil night,
The water is not separate from the waves, and the waves are the water.
When the mirror-like water is untouched by dust or wind, Its manifestations are flawless, illuminating heaven and earth.
Look at me:
pure, naked, and starkly bare, with nothing to grasp. The verse says:
I—recognizing this clearly, two have become one.
Without moving a single hair, one accords with the primordial state; those who know this naturally hear it harmonized with the wind through the pines.
One must strictly avoid following after others. The verse says:
Monkeys cry upon the ridges, cranes call from within the woods; severed clouds are swept by the wind, and waters surge through the long rapids.
Most beloved is the late autumn frost at midnight; A single cry of a new wild goose awakens one to the cold of heaven.
Coming together, they arrive as well. The Verse says:
One breaks into two, forming three; from this they emerge.
Before heaven and earth were divided in their chaotic state, this One was used to bring study and practice to completion;
like a fish drinking water, its coldness or warmth is known by itself. The verse says:
At that time, the clear breeze and bright moon are ever present; the peach is red, the plum is white, and the rose is purple.

When asked about the Lord of the East, he himself knows nothing. Buddha has no face to speak of right or wrong. The verse says: The clear breeze and bright moon are ever present; The peach is red, the plum is white, and the rose is purple.
When asked about the Lord of the East, he himself knows nothing. Buddha has no face to speak of right or wrong. The verse says:
His childhood name was Siddhārtha, his long title Śākyamuni; He delivers countless beings and subdues all manner of heterodoxies.
If you say that another is the Buddha while you yourself have become a demon, I shall simply take this single unperforated flute And blow for you the song of Great Peace.
When a guest arrives, you must observe them; you may not let the opportunity pass, but should strike immediately thereafter. The verse says:
Sitting alone by a single incense burner, Reciting two lines of golden script— How pitiable are those guests in carriages and horses, Left to their own busyness outside the gate.
Śrāvastī (to) the People Together: The Single Hand Does Not Ring Pointlessly. The Verse says:

Sublime and majestic, the King among all dharmas; possessing the thirty-two marks and hundreds of thousands of kinds of light, he is gazed upon by sages and commoners alike, as non-Buddhists submit to him.
"Do not say that a compassionate countenance is difficult to behold.

[This is] a new commentary on the fact that one does not depart from the Great Site of Enlightenment (Mahāmaṇḍala) at Jetavana. The phrase "Thus" (*evam*) refers to the essence of the Dharma heard within this single scripture.
"I have heard" (*śrutam*) means that Ānanda says, "I have heard such a Dharma from the Buddha. "At one time" (*ekasmin samaye*) refers to the occasion when the Tathāgata preached the Dharma.
This is the time when the conditions and responses harmoniously coincide. "Buddha" means "Awakened"; as the Teacher of the Doctrine, his supreme title is Buddha.
Śrāvastī is the name of a kingdom; in the language of China, it means "Abundant Virtue.

Jetavana Anāthapiṇḍada-ārāma refers to Prince Jeta’s donation of trees and the Elder Anāthapiṇḍada’s purchase of the grove, where they together established a vihāra and invited the Buddha to reside there; this is where the teaching was spoken.
The "Dharma-abode" (dharmāyatana) refers to those who are companions for hearing the Dharma. "Bhikṣu" is a term from the Sanskrit;
in the language of China, it means "one who begs" (qishi). He begs above for the Dharma to sustain his life of wisdom, and below for food to sustain his physical body.
Furthermore, he has broken down the banner of self-conceit and generated merit and virtue. "Together with one thousand two hundred and fifty persons" refers to these various [monks].

The disciple has always attended the Buddha wherever he preached the Dharma. These six matters, as listed above, are placed at the beginning of all sutras and are called the "General Preface" (Sādhāraṇa-nidāna).
When the Tathāgata was approaching his parinirvāṇa, Ānanda asked the Buddha what words should be placed at the beginning of all sutras;
the Buddha replied that the words "Thus have I heard" (evam mayā śrutam) and so forth should be placed there.
"It is not only in my teaching that it is thus; all Buddhas of the three periods of time are likewise so.
At that time, at the hour of eating, the World-Honored One put on his robes, took up his alms bowl, and entered the great city of Śrāvastī to beg for food within its walls.
"At that time" refers to this very moment; it indicates that the hour for the midday meal is about to arrive.
"Putting on his robes and taking up his bowl" is done to manifest the traces of his teaching. "Entering" means entering from outside the city.
"The great city of Śrāvastī" is named the City of Abundant Virtue in the kingdom of Śrāvastī; it is where King Prasenajit resides.
Because it was an ancient city, it is called the Great City of Śrāvastī. The term "begging for alms" signifies that the Tathāgata humbles himself before all sentient beings.
Having completed his sequential begging, he returned to his original location; after finishing his meal, he put away his robes and bowl, washed his feet, and spread out a seat.
As for "sitting":
one who follows the sequential method does not discriminate between the poor and the wealthy, but transforms them with impartiality. As for "having finished begging":

if one begs from many houses, it shall not exceed seven; once the count of seven houses is complete, one shall not go to further houses. As for "returning to the original place": [this refers to] the Buddha.
The mind governs all bhikṣus; except when invited, they must not enter the houses of laypeople at will—hence these words.

As for "washing the feet," the Tathāgata manifested this to conform to ordinary people, thus speaking of washing the feet. Furthermore, the Mahāyāna Dharma does not consider purification to consist solely of washing hands and feet;
it implies that cleansing one's hands and feet is not as significant as purifying the mind for a single thought-moment.
When the mind is pure, the defilements of sin are entirely removed. When the Tathāgata wishes to preach the Dharma, it is his constant custom to arrange a sandalwood seat;
therefore, it is said that he "arranged his seat and sat down.
At that time... [until] ...and sat down. *Xingxing* (alertness). The verse says:
Having finished eating and washed his feet, he spreads his seat and sits down; who is it that entrusts [the teaching] to him?
The subsequent text is long—do you know it or not? Look, look! Waves arise upon level ground.
This is a separate narration, also called the "Introductory Narrative" (*nidāna*), which takes the act of begging for alms as its introductory theme.
It is because the Buddha wished to expound upon the giving that is non-abiding in marks (*animitta-dāna*) that he first went for alms to manifest this;

yet, although the Buddha takes the joy of meditation (*dhyānāhāra*) and the joy of the Dharma (*dharmaprīti*) as his sustenance, he goes for alms merely to show himself as being equal to ordinary monks.
"At that time" refers to that specific occasion. "World-Honored One" (*Bhagavat*) is one of the ten titles by which he is revered in the world. "Mealtime" refers to the morning hour.
"Also, 'wearing robes' means donning the *saṃghāṭī*; 'carrying an alms bowl' means holding the appropriate vessel;
'begging in sequence' means that the Buddha’s mind is impartial, making no distinction between the poor and the wealthy; 'the original location' refers to Anāthapiṇḍada’s Park;
'washing the feet' is because in India one eats barefoot, and thus washes the feet after the meal; 'spreading out a seat'..."
"Sitting" refers to spreading out the sitting mat and assuming the full lotus posture (paryaṅka).
Section Two: The Inquiry of Subhūti.
Because this section both reveals wisdom arising from emptiness and provides the response thereto, it follows [the preceding section] with the "Inquiry of Subhūti."
At that time, there was the Elder Subhūti.

Why is he called "Elder"? Because his virtue is honored and his years are advanced, he is thus named the Elder Subhūti; this is a Sanskrit term whose meaning in the language of Tang (Chinese) is "One Who Understands Emptiness."

Amidst the great assembly, he immediately rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in reverent salutation, and addressed the Buddha, saying:
"Because one follows the seating arrangement of sentient beings, it is said that 'he immediately rose from his seat. A disciple seeking instruction first performs these five kinds of [prostrations]."

The ritual procedure consists of five steps: first, rising from one’s seat; second, adjusting and straightening one’s robes; third, baring the right shoulder and placing the right knee upon the ground;
fourth, joining the palms and gazing up at the Honored One’s countenance without averting the eyes for even a moment;
and fifth, inquiring with a single mind of reverence.
"How rare, World-Honored One!
How rare is this brief exposition of the three meanings: first, how most rare is the ability to renounce the sovereignty of a Golden Wheel-Turning King;

second, how rare is a body one *zhang* and six *chi* tall with the luster of purple-polished gold, adorned with the thirty-two major marks and eighty minor signs; third, [the rarity of] the Three Realms..."
The third rare quality, "Incomparable," refers to the capacity to encompass and expound the eighty-four thousand dharmas and the perfect completion of the three bodies (trikāya).
Because it possesses these three aforementioned meanings, it is called "rare. As for "World-Honored One" (Lokanātha): his wisdom transcends the triple world such that none can equal it;
his virtue is so exalted that there is nothing superior to it, and all pay him reverence. Therefore, he is called "World-Honored One."
World-Honored One, the Tathāgata well protects and sustains all bodhisattvas and well entrusts all bodhisattvas.
As for "protecting and sustaining," it means that the Tathāgata protects and sustains all bodhisattvas through the Dharma of the *prajñāpāramitā*. As for "entrusting," [it means...]
The Tathāgata, through the Dharma of Prajñāpāramitā, entrusts it to Subhūti and the great Bodhisattvas, saying:

"Guard and cherish them well. This means that he causes all practitioners to protect their own minds through the wisdom of Prajñā, so that they do not give rise to deluded attachments of hatred or love toward the six external sense objects, nor fall into the ocean of suffering of birth and death; rather, they maintain mindfulness within their own hearts.
"Maintain constant right mindfulness so that no wrong thoughts arise; this is the Tathāgata’s own nature of self-protection and care.

To speak of 'well-entrusting' means that when the preceding thought is pure, it is entrusted to the succeeding thought, and as each succeeding thought remains pure without interruption, one attains ultimate liberation.
The Tathāgata has thus provided detailed instructions for sentient beings and the assembly gathered here: you should always practice this."

Therefore, it is said that they are "well entrusted. A *bodhisattva*—a term from the Sanskrit, translated in Chinese as "one with the mind of the Way" (*daoxin zhongsheng*) or "enlightened sentient being" (*jue youqing*)—is so called because they constantly practice reverence and universally respect and love all living beings down to the most minute insects, never harboring a heart of contempt or arrogance;
hence, they are named a *bodhisattva*.
At that time, from the Elder [Subhūti] up to all the bodhisattvas, the Tathāgata did not utter a single word; Subhūti then offered this praise:
"O you of superior lineage who possess the divine eye, please cast your gaze upon us! The verse says:
Seeing a horn over a wall, one knows it is an ox; seeing smoke from behind a mountain, one knows it is fire.
Sitting alone and majestic above heaven and under heaven—north, south, east, and west! To probe the tortoise shell and strike the tiles! *Du!* (A shout of realization).
New Commentary: The Elder Subhūti is the one who initiated this sutra. He is called "Elder" because his virtue is mature and he is advanced in years.
In Sanskrit he is Subhūti; in the language of China, he is translated as "Born of Emptiness" (Kōngshēng) and is also named "Well-Appeared" (Shànxiàn).
From "rising from his seat" to "reverently," these terms signify the respect shown when requesting the Dharma. "Rare" (*āścarya*) is a term used to praise the Buddha.

Regarding "skillfully protecting and mindful of": it means to protect and mindfully care for those bodhisattvas of the present whose faculties are mature, using the power of wisdom to bring them to full maturity through their own practice, and using the power of teaching and transformation to cause them to gather in and sustain sentient beings.
Regarding "skillfully entrusting": it means to entrust those bodhisattvas of the future whose faculties are not yet mature, who have already attained the Mahāyāna, so that they may...
Not abandoning those who have not yet attained the Mahāyāna so as to cause them to advance further—this act of protective mindfulness and entrustment is indeed a rare occurrence.
Although the Buddha’s virtue is supreme, it does not exceed that which concerns sentient beings;

yet, even while focusing his attention on the Prajñāpāramitā to deliver beings, he necessarily awaits questions. Therefore, Subhūti, perceiving the signs and understanding his intention, first praised this as rare before [proceeding].
I ask: World-Honored One, regarding good sons and good daughters—what is meant by a "good son"?
It is one whose mind is level and even, and who possesses a mind of right concentration; such a person is able to accomplish all things.
Wherever merit goes, it is unimpeded. A "good woman" is one whose mind possesses right wisdom;
from this mind of right wisdom, all conditioned and unconditioned merits can be produced.
"How should one who has set out on the path toward *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* abide? How should they subdue their mind?
Subhūti asks how all those who have generated the bodhicitta should abide and how they should subdue their minds.
Subhūti, observing that the minds of all sentient beings are restless and ceaseless— like dust motes flickering in a crevice,
their agitated thoughts arising like whirling winds and continuing from moment to moment without interruption— he asked how one who wishes to practice should subdue them.
"Bhagavān, [up to] 'his mind'—from where does this question arise? The verse says:
"You rejoice, but I do not rejoice; You grieve, but I do not grieve.
The wild goose longs to fly north to the cold; The swallow remembers its old nest and returns."
"The infinite meaning of autumn moons and spring flowers—within this, only one may know it for oneself.
(New Commentary: This is the opening of the inquiry. *Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* is translated into Chinese as "Unsurpassed, Right, Equal, and Perfect Enlightenment.
The intent of the question concerns the Tathāgata’s protective mindfulness and entrustment in the present.
Regarding the future attainment of Buddhahood by Bodhisattvas: although these Bodhisattvas have resolved their minds on the Way, vowed to deliver all sentient beings,
and sought the path to Buddhahood, it is not yet known how their minds abide within the Mahāyāna,
nor how they subdue deluded thoughts so as to reach the fruit of Buddhahood without falling back or losing their way.
The Buddha said, "Excellent, excellent, Subhūti! It is as you have said:
the Tathāgata well protects and mindfully sustains all bodhisattvas, and well entrusts all bodhisattvas.
This was the Buddha praising Subhūti for having perfectly grasped his heart and perfectly grasped his intent.
Listen attentively now, and I shall speak for you.
Whenever the Buddha intends to preach the Dharma, he first invariably exhorts those who listen to maintain single-minded silence, saying, "I shall now speak for you."
Good sons and good daughters who have resolved their minds on *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* should abide in this way and subdue their minds in this way.
"An" means non-existent; "uttara" means above; "sam" means correct; "yak" means pervasive; "bodhi" means...
"Ti" means knowing that which is non-existent; "wu" means being free from all defilements; "shang" means that within the three realms there is nothing with which it can be compared;
"zheng" refers to right view; "bian" refers to universal wisdom;
and "zhi" refers to knowing that all sentient beings possess Buddha-nature and that by practicing cultivation, they will all attain Buddhahood. These three are the unsurpassed, pure Prajñā.
The pāramitās are likewise; therefore, if any good sons or good daughters wish to practice,
they should know the path to unsurpassed bodhi and should know the dharma of the unsurpassed, pure prajñāpāramitā,
using this to subdue their minds.
"Yes, indeed, World-Honored One; we wish and desire to hear.
"Yes, indeed" is a phrase of assent. "Wish and desire" means wishing that the Buddha would explain extensively so that those of middling and inferior faculties may all attain awakening.
"Desire" means delighting in hearing the profound Dharma. "Wish to hear" means thirsting for and yearning for the compassionate instruction.
The Buddha said: “Stop, stop! Listen to the causes and conditions of these matters as I instruct you. He spoke in verse:
Seven hands and eight feet, divine heads and demonic faces— A staff cannot open them, a blade cannot sever them.
They leap and bound across Jambudvīpa thousands of times; Yet in every instance, they do not leave the Hall of the Empty King.
New Commentary: Since Subhūti had praised and inquired [about the Dharma] in a manner that perfectly accorded with the Buddha’s mind, the Buddha confirmed it, saying, "Excellent, excellent!
I shall explain it for you. Furthermore, he cautioned him, saying, "You should abide thus;
you should subdue your mind thus. Subhūti immediately understood the Buddha’s intention and responded, "So be it," expressing his wish to hear this Dharma.
However, the essential purport of this sutra does not exceed what Subhūti asked regarding abiding in the Mahāyāna and subduing the deluded mind,
and what the Tathāgata answered concerning the methods of practice; these likewise do not go beyond the two modes of conduct— principle and phenomena—
and the refutation of attachments and severance of doubts, as will be fully seen in the following text.
Section Three: The Orthodox Tradition of the Mahāyāna.

This tradition transcends the distinction between the orthodox and the heterodox; while there are no fixed categories of Great or Small Vehicles, beings are transformed and delivered according to their three levels of capacity.
Because it sets aside divergent doctrines and stands alone as supreme, it is followed by the Section on the Orthodox Tradition of the Mahāyāna.
The Buddha told Subhūti: "All bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should subdue their minds in this way.

When the preceding thought is pure and the subsequent thought is pure, this is called a bodhisattva whose every thought does not regress. Although they remain amidst the dust and toil of the world, their minds are constantly pure;
thus they are called mahāsattvas. Through the various skillful means of the [four] immeasurables—loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity—they transform sentient beings."
To deliver sentient beings is called being a Bodhisattva; when the mind has no attachment toward either the transformer or the transformed, this is called a Mahāsattva.
To revere all sentient beings is precisely to subdue one's own mind. That which is real (*tathatā*) does not change; that which is suchness (*tathā*) does not differ.
Encountering various objective realms, the mind remains without alteration—this is termed "Suchness" (*tathatā*). It is also said that externally it is not... [text truncated].

To call something "provisional" means it is not real; to say the internal is not empty means it is as-it-is (*tathatā*). That every thought-moment is without deviation is precisely what it means to subdue the mind.
(The phrase "not empty" is in one edition rendered as "not disordered.
[New Commentary: Subhūti asked about both abiding and subduing, yet the Tathāgata answered only regarding the subduing of the mind.
One who skillfully subdues the deluded mind and abides in the Mahāyāna shall then receive those who abide therein.
All classes of sentient beings—whether born from eggs, born from wombs, born from moisture, or born by transformation—[are likewise included].
New Commentary: Humans and animals possess all four modes of birth (*yoni*). Among the various heavens, hells, and intermediate states (*antarābhava*), there is only apparitional birth (*upapāduka*).
Ghosts (*preta*) admit of both womb-born and apparitional births; all of these belong to the Desire Realm (*kāmadhātu*).

There are three kinds of giving: the gift of material resources, the gift of fearlessness, and the gift of the Dharma. The gift of material resources consists of bestowing wealth and goods to sustain the lives of others.

The gift of fearlessness consists of maintaining the precepts so as not to cause distress, and practicing patience toward those who bear no enmity or toward those who harbor enmity, without seeking retaliation.
The gift of the Dharma consists of preaching the teachings with tireless diligence and expounding the Dharma through meditative concentration that is perfectly attuned to the capacities of listeners.

it is the sentient-being world when there are afflictions within the mind. Because one realizes that all deluded thoughts are empty and quiescent, it is said: "It is not a world.

Having realized the Dharmakāya of the Tathāgata, one universally perceives all lands within atoms; its responsive applications (*upāya*) are without fixed direction—this is what is meant by [the name].
The World. Subhūti...

With one hand pointing to heaven and the other treading upon the earth, when hungry one eats, and when weary one sleeps.

The meaning of this passage follows from the previous section on obtaining blessings through the bestowal of jewels; for it is immeasurable.

these atoms are insentient objects that do not give rise to the causes of defilement such as greed; thus, conditioned meritorious retribution cannot even equal those atoms.
Is it not the case that upholding and reciting this sutra is the cause for distancing oneself from afflictions and attaining bodhi?
That which is neither atoms nor worlds is not the cause of defilement by afflictions;
rather, these atoms and worlds are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). "Indeterminate" refers to that which is insentient, meaning they do not give rise to good or evil.
"Subhūti, what do you think? Can the Tathāgata be seen by means of the thirty-two marks?

If one does not cultivate the practices of purity for the thirty-two marks, one will ultimately not become a Buddha.
Merely craving and being attached to the Tathāgata’s thirty-two marks, while not personally cultivating the practices for the thirty-two marks, will ultimately prevent one from seeing the Tathāgata.
Subhūti (up to) the Two Marks: Borrowing a *śāṇa* robe to bow for one’s mother-in-law’s birthday. The verse says: You have it, and I also have it;
when you lack it, I also lack it. Neither existence nor non-existence can be established; facing each other, we are like *zīlúdu*.
New Commentary: The thirty-two marks are the characteristics of the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body); that which is "not a mark" is the characteristic of the *dharmakāya* (dharma body).

That which is called the "thirty-two marks" refers to the fact that when there is an occasion for response, the Buddha responds accordingly; thus, it does not preclude speaking of the thirty-two marks.

Although the merit of bestowing jewels may enable one to attain the physical characteristics of a Buddha's body, this is merely the *nirmāṇakāya* and cannot compare to [the merit of] upholding and expounding [this sutra].
Merit is able to accomplish the substance of the Dharma-body.
Subhūti, if there are good men or good women who give their body and life as many times as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River in alms,
yet another person were to take up even a single four-line verse from this sutra and explain it to others—
The merit thereof is exceedingly great.
Among all things held dear in the world, none surpasses one's own body and life.

Although the merit of a Bodhisattva who, for the sake of the Dharma, relinquishes their body and life to all sentient beings throughout immeasurable kalpas is vast, it does not equal that of receiving, upholding, and reciting this sutra.
The merit of these four lines is such that even if one were to sacrifice their body over many kalpas, they would not yet comprehend the meaning of emptiness nor eliminate the deluded mind;

being fundamentally a sentient being, by upholding this sutra for a single thought-moment, the notions of self and person are instantly exhausted. Once delusive thoughts are eliminated, one becomes a Buddha in the very moment of speaking.
Therefore, know that sacrificing the body over many kalpas is not equal to the merit of upholding these four lines of the sutra.
Subhūti, it is exceedingly much; two colors, one match. The verse says:
The humble hand, the slippery mallet, the unchanging sword— Those who are skilled in their use find them all at hand.
No need for contrivance; they are originally perfected. Within this, there must be a man of heroic spirit.
Ra ra ri ri ra ra. When mountain flowers laugh and wild birds sing, if one attains the true meaning at this moment, then wherever one may be—*svāhā*.
(New Commentary) Bestowing the seven treasures is the gift of external wealth; bestowing one's body and life is the gift of internal wealth. The gift of the body...
The former is like King Śibi who gave himself in place of a dove; the latter is like the Sattva who fed a tiger.

Comparing these by way of their relative weight, external wealth is light and easy to give, while internal wealth is heavy and difficult to give. Nevertheless, both of these two types of giving are conditioned and tainted (*sāsrava*);
in terms of cause and effect, they are generally not equal to upholding and reciting even a single four-line verse, which can lead one to attain Bodhi.
This is the wondrous fruit. ○ Chapter Fourteen:
The Section on Detachment from Characteristics and Quiescent Extinction.

Because one hears the sutra, understands its meaning, and uniquely awakens to the true reality (*bhūtatathatā*), it is followed by the section on detachment from characteristics and quiescent extinction.
At that time, having heard this sutra being preached, Subhūti deeply understood its meaning and intent; he wept with tears of sorrow and said to the Buddha:

"It is rare, World-Honored One! Regarding such a profound sutra as the Buddha has preached, from my past until now, though I have attained the eye of wisdom, I have never before heard a sutra such as this."
At that time... [the text] of the sutra. It is laughable that one should face such avoidance; the verse says:
Having been accustomed to traveling to distant lands since childhood, How many times have I crossed the Xiang River at Mount Heng?
Now, once treading the path home, I realize for the first time how long the days and months were on the road.
World-Honored One, if there should be anyone who hears this sutra and their faith becomes pure and clear, they will give rise to true reality;
you should know that such a person accomplishes the foremost and most rare merit.
The absence of delusion regarding intrinsic nature is called the eye of wisdom; hearing the Dharma and awakening to it for oneself is called the Dharma-eye.

Subhūti, as an arhat among five hundred disciples, was foremost in understanding emptiness. Having already diligently served many buddhas in the past, how could he not have heard such profound teachings?
How could one say that he first heard them only from Śākyamuni Buddha?
However, it may be that Subhūti had previously attained only the wisdom-eye of a śrāvaka, and it was only now that he realized the Buddha’s intent;
thus, for the first time, he was able to hear such a profound sutra. Mourning his former lack of realization, he wept with tears of sorrow.
Hearing the sutra, he contemplated it with focused mindfulness, declaring it to be pure. From within this pure essence, the Prajñāpāramitā flows forth.
One should know that this profound Dharma of the *pāramitās* definitively accomplishes the merits of all Buddhas.
World-Honored One, that which is the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) is itself the absence of marks; therefore, the Tathāgata speaks of it by the name "true mark."
Although one may practice pure conduct, if one perceives the two aspects of defilement and purity, both are in fact defiled within the mind;
this is not the pure mind. Whenever the mind has anything to grasp, it is not the true mark (dharmatā).
The World-Honored One [reaches] the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). From where do the mountains, rivers, and the great earth come?
The verse says: Gazing afar, the mountains have color; Listening closely, the waters have no sound.
Spring has passed, yet the flowers remain; People arrive, but the birds are not startled.
Every single thing is fully revealed; in every object, the fundamental essence is level and even.
How can one say they do not understand? It is simply because it is too clear.
World-Honored One, for me now to hear such a sutra as this, and to believe, understand, accept, and uphold it, is not difficult.
It is difficult for the World-Honored One [to speak]; if the subsequent words are not obtained, the preceding words cannot be made complete. The verse says:
Difficult, difficult, difficult— Like a clear blue sky over level ground, Easy, easy, easy— Like falling asleep while still wearing one’s clothes.
The sailing of a boat depends entirely upon the helmsman; who would say that waves and billows arise from the earth?

Likewise, in the future age of the final five hundred years, if there are sentient beings who hear this sutra and, with faith and understanding, accept and uphold it, such persons shall be the most rare and extraordinary of all.
If it were truly rare [to encounter], what further matter would there be in walking, standing, sitting, lying down, putting on clothes, or eating food?
The verse says:

If a person can believe this, they will look south at the Big Dipper.

Why is this? The mark of a self is itself no-mark; the mark of a person, the mark of a sentient being, and the mark of a life-span are themselves no-marks.
Why? Because the relinquishing of all marks is what is called "all Buddhas."

Subhūti has profoundly realized the Buddha’s intent; having personally seen that his karma is exhausted and defilements removed, his wisdom-eye is clear and penetrating, so that he can believe, understand, accept, and uphold [the teaching] without difficulty.

Even during the time when the World-Honored One was present in the world and the Dharma was flourishing, there were immeasurable sentient beings who could not believe, understand, accept, or uphold it—why then speak only of the final five hundred years? This is because while the Buddha was in the world...
On this day, although there were those of middling and inferior capacities who lacked faith or harbored doubts, they immediately went to question the Buddha;

the Buddha then taught them according to their needs, and there was none who did not attain realization. After the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, during the latter five hundred years as the Dharma gradually enters the age of decline, we are far removed from the Sage and only the verbal teachings remain.

Though the bamboo be dense, it does not hinder the flowing stream; though the mountain be high, how could it obstruct the flying white clouds?

King Kali, King Kali.

When the Tathāgata was on the first bhūmi during his causal stage, while he was a kṣānti-rṣi, King Kali cut off his limbs and body;
yet he did not harbor even a single thought of pain or affliction. Had he harbored a thought of pain or affliction, anger and resentment would have arisen.
"Kali" is a Sanskrit term, which here means "an unrighteous and extremely evil ruler. According to one tradition, this refers to the Tathāgata’s causal stage.
In a former life, he was a king who constantly practiced the ten wholesome deeds and benefited all living beings;
because the people of his kingdom sang praises of this king, he is called King Kali. Seeking supreme bodhi, he cultivated the practice of patience.

At that time, Śakra, Lord of the Devas, transformed himself into a *caṇḍāla* and begged for the flesh of the king’s body; the king cut it off and gave it away without the slightest anger or resentment. Two [verses] remain here.
This is explained as being consistent with both principles.
Subhūti further recalled that in the past, for five hundred lifetimes, he had been a rishi of forbearance;
during all those lifetimes, there was no mark of a self, no mark of a person, no mark of a sentient being, and no mark of a life-span.
The Tathāgata, while in the causal stage, practiced the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) for five hundred lifetimes in order to attain the four marks of non-arising.
When the Tathāgata describes his own causal nature, he does so desiring that all practitioners of the path may achieve the perfection of patience;
for once a practitioner of patience has already practiced this perfection, they will not... [be hindered].
Seeing the faults and evils of all people, one regards enemies and kin with equanimity, being neither partial nor antagonistic;
when struck, reviled, or harmed by others, one accepts it with joy and redoubles one's respect. One who practices in this manner is able to accomplish the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).
Why is this so? As for the characteristics [of this state]: before one's eyes there is no dharma; though willows are green and flowers are red, nothing is heard by the ear.
Let the warbling of the oriole and the chatter of the swallow be as they may. The verse says:
The four great elements are fundamentally without self; The five aggregates all return to emptiness and vast vacancy.
In principle, heaven and earth remain as they have for ten thousand ages;
The wondrous peak stands towering, ever as it was. Who cares for the winds that howl wildly, shaking the very earth?

New Commentary: Patience (*kṣānti*) is one of the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*). To accept [injury] with equanimity is called "patience" (*kṣānti*); to be harmed or injured is called "insult" (*māna*).

The Dharma is non-self; reaching the other shore while teaching what is not the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*) is precisely to eliminate attachment.

Such practice of patience was practiced by the Buddha in former times; therefore, he cites the incident of King Kali to verify it. In Sanskrit, King Kali is called "the Extremely Wicked" (*atikrūra*);
in the Flower Language (Chinese), it means "extremely evil. In a previous life, the Buddha was once a rishi who cultivated the Way in the mountains.
When the king, while out hunting, saw him and was displeased, he cut off his ears and nose and severed his hands and feet;
yet the seer felt not the slightest resentment, and by the power of his compassion and forbearance, his body was restored to its former state.

This is because he had thoroughly realized that the four marks—the self, the person, the sentient being, and the life-span—are all empty; thus, not only was there no suffering, but there was even joy. Furthermore, it is cited:

The fact that he acted as a Rishi of Forbearance throughout five hundred past lives to provide this testimony clarifies that the practice of the path of forbearance does not pertain to a single lifetime alone. Therefore,
Subhūti, a bodhisattva should depart from all marks and give rise to *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
The Bodhicitta. Therefore, [it is said]: "This is the function; it is separate from this function. The verse says:
"Attaining it in the mind, responding with the hand; Like snow, moon, wind, and flowers; as long as heaven and earth endure."
Every morning the cock cries out at the fifth watch; spring arrives and mountain flowers bloom everywhere.

One should not give rise to the mind by dwelling on forms, nor should one give rise to the mind by dwelling on sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, or dharmas. One should give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere.
"One should not give rise to a mind dwelling on form" is the general heading; "sound, fragrance," and so forth, are the specific enumeration of their names.

When one gives rise to feelings of aversion or attachment toward these six objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*), the mind thereby accumulates immeasurable karmic fetters, which shroud the Buddha-nature (*buddhadhātu*).
Thus, even if one practices with various kinds of diligent hardship, if the defilements of the mind are not removed, there is no principle of liberation.

If one traces its root, it all stems from the mind abiding within form. If one can practice the *prajñāpāramitā* at every thought-moment, one will realize that all phenomena are empty and not give rise to attachment.
At every thought-moment, one should always be diligent and single-mindedly guard [the mind] so as not to become negligent.
As the *Vimalakīrtinirdeśa Sūtra* says: "One seeks all-knowledge above; there is no seeking of the Great [Vehicle] that is not done at the proper time."

The Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra states: "A bodhisattva mahāsattva, day and night, applies themselves with diligence, constantly abiding in mental engagement associated with the prajñāpāramitā, never relinquishing it for even a moment."
If the mind has a dwelling, it is a non-dwelling.

Not dwelling in nirvana, not dwelling in any phenomena, and not dwelling in any location—this alone is the dwelling place of a bodhisattva. As stated in the preceding passage, one should dwell nowhere. And yet...

Therefore, the Buddha said: "Subhūti, a bodhisattva’s mind should not dwell on form when practicing giving.
A bodhisattva, for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, should practice giving in this manner."
A bodhisattva does not practice giving for the sake of seeking personal happiness;
rather, they practice giving in order to internally destroy the mind of stinginess and externally benefit all sentient beings.
One should not [refuse] alms; one must not stay where there is a Buddha, nor pass by in haste where there is no Buddha.
After thirty years have passed, do not say you did not know. The verse says:
Wandering South Mountain in the morning, staying at Tiantai in the evening; pursuing him, he cannot be caught, yet he comes of his own accord.
Walking alone and sitting alone, free from all constraints; where the mind finds room, there one should find room.
The Tathāgata says that all marks are non-marks; he further says that all sentient beings are not truly sentient beings.
"Birth. That which is such (*tathatā*) is not born; that which comes does not perish. That which is not born is the non-arising of self and person;
that which does not perish is awakening-illumination. As the subsequent passage states: "The Tathāgata comes from nowhere and goes nowhere; therefore he is called [Tathāgata]."
The Tathāgata, as the Tathāgata, has taught that the marks of a self, a person, and so forth are ultimately destructible and lack a real essence.
All sentient beings are merely provisional designations; if one is separated from the deluded mind, no sentient being can be found.
Therefore, it is said that they are "not indeed sentient beings."
From the Tathāgata down to ordinary beings, there is a distinct excellence that need not be withheld; it may be brought forth. The verse says:
Neither being nor appearance, In spring warmth, the yellow oriole sings atop the willows.

hence it is said: "One should not dwell on form while practicing giving. Practicing giving in this manner is for the benefit [of others].

Subhūti, the Tathāgata is one who speaks the truth, one who speaks reality, one who speaks according to suchness, one who does not speak deceptively, and one who does not speak otherwise.
As one who speaks the truth, he declares that all sentient beings and non-sentient things possess Buddha-nature; as one who speaks reality, he declares to the assembly...

This subtle and wondrous speech of the Buddha cannot be surpassed or destroyed by any heavenly Māras or non-Buddhist paths.

Functioning in emptiness without interruption, one cannot say it is non-existent, nor can one say it is existent;

My son Nan’guo has returned home with virtue; his family members have honored me by commissioning the transcription of this supreme vehicle scripture using paper and brush.

He has ordered artisans to carve the printing blocks and distribute them for circulation at Xulin Dutan Dongji Monastery. May this act above repay the four debts of gratitude and below sustain the three realms of existence.
It is my universal aspiration that all sentient beings may together clarify the cause of Prajñā and ultimately enter the Golden Land.
On this day of the Earthly Branch of Geng, I humbly pray that my late father, the deceased Lord Qianwu Jianwu Zhugong,
my late mother, Lady Min (the "Hundred-Three" Lady), and all those who have been my karmic relatives throughout successive generations,
may rely upon these virtuous causes and together ascend to the realm of the Buddhas.
The Mantra for Supplementation:
*Namo ratnatrayāya kha ra kha ra ma ra ma ra hu ra hūṃ ha ha sūtana hūṃ sphoṭa na phaṭ svāhā*.
